1:
Gill reads the note about there being no king as an explanation offered in advance, the period lying after Joshua and before Othniel, so that the theft of Micah's priest and his gods, and the setting up of the image in Dan, spread an idolatry which brought on the servitude Othniel was raised to end. On the tribe's landlessness Ellicott is precise: the inheritance had been assigned, but they had not been able to conquer it against the Philistines and the Amorites, and the English version interpolates the words all their before inheritance to smooth the difficulty — a well-meant gloss, but such glosses violate the translator's first duty, which is to be rigidly faithful. He finds the failure the more remarkable because in the wilderness Dan had been the strongest of all the tribes and had received the smallest allotment of any. Henry supplies the motive, that the city lay far off and wholly in enemy hands, so they preferred to sponge upon their brethren until necessity roused them — better, he adds, to have a little of one's own than always to hang upon others.

The choice of scouts is admired. Henry notes that they were men of valour who, if they fell into enemy hands, knew how to look danger in the face, and that it is prudent to look before we leap; Dan had the subtlety of a serpent as well as the courage of a lion's whelp. Clarke observes that the Hebrew word covers personal prowess, mental energy and earthly substance alike, and that they sent men in whose judgment and prudence they could confide. Keil takes the phrase about their coasts to mean out of their whole body.

How they knew the Levite is disputed. Clarke and Keil both make it a matter of speech — Clarke that they knew by his pronunciation that he was no Ephraimite, the tribe having already been caught out by a syllable, and Keil that his dialect showed him no native of those mountains. Ellicott thinks acquaintance more likely than accent, since Jonathan had lived at Bethlehem, the grandson of Moses can hardly have been wholly unknown, and Dan and Judah had close intercourse then. His own preference is that they recognised him by hearing him at his service before the image; and he records Cassel's rendering of the word as sound rather than voice, referred to the bells of the priestly dress.

The consultation divides them sharply. Henry has no patience with it: they would never have enquired of God at all had the sight of the teraphim not put it into their heads, like the many who never think of religion except when it falls in their way; and they supposed that God, having forbidden graven images, would answer them through one. He notes that they had passed Shiloh without enquiring of the high priest there, thinking better of Micah's teraphim than of God's urim, and that the Levite, whether he believed it himself or not, humoured them so well that they took his word for God's. Ellicott agrees they might at least have consulted Phinehas, and hears in the reply the ambiguity of an oracle, Jonathan staking nothing on any definite detail. Gill leaves the door open both ways, that the priest spoke either of his own head or by a voice which Satan might be permitted to deliver. Clarke argues the opposite case and names those he is arguing against. The Danites say Elohim and the priest answers before Jehovah, a name never given to any but the true God; the venture succeeded exactly as the oracle said; and it is begging the question to call the answer a trick of the Levite or a suggestion of the devil and the success accidental, which is to take the thing by the worst handle to prop up a system.
7:
Henry says of Laish that never was a place so ill governed nor so ill guarded. The want of a magistrate he takes for the heart of it: rulers are heirs of restraint, entrusted with an entail of power for the checking of what is evil, and though only grace can renew a depraved mind, the magistrate's hand may tie it, so that the wickedness of the wicked is neither so injurious nor so infectious as it would else be. He notes the method the verse names, that of putting men to shame, so that those not held back by the shamefulness of the sin may be held by the shamefulness of the punishment. Ellicott finds the clause almost unreadable and suspects the text corrupt, the versions differing widely; as it stands he takes it to mean that no one possessing wealth among them did harm in any matter, the Greek giving heir of treasure.

On their security all three agree and differ only in the reason. Henry has their gates open and their walls out of repair, under no apprehension though their wickedness gave them reason to fear vengeance daily; and he reads it as a sign that Israel, through sloth and cowardice, was no longer the terror to Canaan it had been. Being an open inland town they yet lived like the Zidonians, who had the sea about them and were fortified by art and nature — but far from those Zidonians, who could not come to their aid. Their having no business with any man he takes either for idleness, since they followed no trade and so grew unable to defend themselves, or for the independency they affected, scorning subjection and alliance alike: they cared for nobody, and so nobody cared for them. Clarke and Ellicott both suppose them a colony from Sidon imitating the mother city's ease without her defences, and Clarke draws the military conclusion, that they could be struck before the news of invasion reached Sidon. On the last clause Clarke prefers the Greek, which reads that they had no dealings with Syria: Aram and Adam differ by a single letter often indiscernible in manuscript, and Laish lay on the Syrian frontier, so that its isolation from the one neighbour that could have relieved it becomes a further reason for the Danites' confidence.

Ellicott places the town: it is the Leshem of Joshua, now Tel el-Kadi, the mound of the judge, northernmost city of Palestine, at the head of the chief stream of the Jordan; its position on a round hill girt with trees bears out the description entirely, so the spies' verdict that the land was very good needs no discounting. He renders the large land as wide on both hands, which Keil explains as room both to settle and to spread.

Henry credits the spies with honesty. The tribe had formed notions of insuperable difficulty and kept out of its own possession accordingly, and the report was framed with that discouragement in view — these, he says, were not in this evil spies. Keil renders their opening as a rebuke, that the brethren stand silent, and traces their confidence that God had given the place into their hands back to the Levite's oracle; Ellicott agrees that the inference rests on nothing else. Clarke calls the speech plain and nervous, and observes that it took effect at once. Of the six hundred he notes that these were the armed men only; Ellicott renders appointed as girded and insists this was no raid but the migration of a section of the tribe with wives, children and goods. Gill measures the stages from Bunting, sixteen miles to Kirjath-jearim for the first day's march and eight more to mount Ephraim. Keil and Ellicott both reason from the permanence of the name Mahaneh-dan that the halt was no single night's bivouac but a stay of some length.
14:
Keil puts the spies' hint plainly: do not lose this chance of getting a worship of our own for the new settlement. Clarke suspects the design of carrying off priest and furniture was formed already, and Ellicott glosses the invitation to consider as meaning whether and how to possess themselves of the things — finding in these Danite freebooters the mixture of superstition with lawlessness, of robbery with devotion, often remarked in Greek and Italian brigands. Henry grants one point and denies the rest. It was right to want God's presence, but wretchedly wrong to take for tokens of it images fitter for a puppet-play than for devotion; they wanted an oracle for company and for a council of war, and reckoned that men settling so far from Shiloh had more need of a house of gods than Micah, who lived close by it. Only the reputation the things had lately acquired amused them into a veneration they would have dropped at once had they thought to ask where the images came from.

How the priest came to be outside while his sanctuary was emptied is answered three ways. Gill reconstructs a manoeuvre: the five went first to the house, saluted the young man, told him a body of their brethren at the gate would be glad to see him, and walked him down; then, having introduced him, slipped back. Keil notices that the grammar answers the same difficulty, the narrative passing into perfects which do not carry the story forward but set the coming and the taking inside the same stretch of time as the priest's standing at the gate — though he still finds it surprising that the man stood there while the robbery went on. Henry gives no manoeuvre, only negligence: while he sauntered at the gate and gazed at the strangers his treasure was gone. Keil observes that the five went up, so Micah's house of God must have occupied an upper room; Ellicott suggests the ephod habitually hung upon the carved image, so that whoever carried off the one carried off the other.

Henry turns the theft into an indictment. See how impotent these gods were, that could not keep themselves from being stolen — it is the reproach of idols elsewhere that they have themselves gone into captivity — and how sottish the Danites, to think such protectors could protect them. Their idolatry began in theft, a fit prologue to such an opera: to break the second commandment they began with the eighth, taking a neighbour's goods to make them their gods, and though the holy God hates robbery for burnt offering, the devil loves it.

The buying of the priest is told with relish. Henry sets out the terms as preferment: it is more honour and more profit to be chaplain to a regiment — for a regiment was all they were, though they called themselves a tribe — than domestic chaplain to a private gentleman, and he would have more dependants, more sacrifices and more fees than he had where he was. On the gesture that opened the negotiation Clarke and Ellicott reach for the same iconography, Clarke naming Harpocrates, the god of silence, shown with a finger pressed to his lips, and Ellicott the Egyptian Horus. Gill reads the gladness of the priest's heart as of a piece with a covetous and unsettled temper; Ellicott is harsher, calling the alacrity with which he sanctions the theft very unworthy of a grandson of Moses, and setting beside it Dean Stanley's parallel of the bribe offered in 1176 to the monk Roger of Canterbury — give us the portion of St Thomas's skull in thy keeping, and thou shalt be no simple monk but an abbot. Clarke has him step into the crowd so as not to be spotted by Micah's household; Ellicott, that the people closed round to guard him.
21:
The order of march betrays what kind of expedition this was. Keil notes that the children, cattle and valuables went in front because the Danites feared an attack from the rear, and takes the word for little ones to include the women; Ellicott observes that it is only in this incidental way that the narrative lets slip that a whole migration is on the road. Clarke reads the same confidence in it, that men so sure of success removed families, goods and cattle together. On the last item in the list the three divide. Clarke gives first the sense of substance or precious things, which the Vulgate has as everything that was precious, but prefers the baggage, what Caesar calls impedimenta and the Greek renders weight — and he warns that no wheeled carriage is to be imagined. Ellicott sets the same two readings side by side, the Alexandrine manuscript giving their glorious possession and the Vatican the weight, and inclines to the latter on the ground that the root means to be heavy. Keil decides flatly the other way: the valuables, and not the heavy baggage.

The pursuit is timed by two of them. Gill allows an interval before Micah even knew that his gods were gone and his priest decoyed away, and a further interval to collect servants and neighbours; Ellicott adds why the overtaking was easy, since the Danite march was slowed by women, children and cattle, and remarks that Micah's establishment was probably strong enough against ordinary robbers, but that nobody could have looked for a raid of six hundred. Keil reads the two clauses of the verse as circumstantial, so that the calling out and the overtaking are the setting rather than the action. Ellicott hears grim humour in the exchange, with a note of irony at Micah's complete discomfiture, and finds Dan behaving exactly as the blessing had described him, a serpent on the way and an adder in the path.

The phrase my gods which I made is what the commentators fasten on. Gill points out that ownership was the best argument Micah had and a poor one for their divinity, and thinks it astonishing that a man should call them gods when he knew their making and had seen they could not save themselves from theft. Clarke will not allow the word its worst sense: Micah being a worshipper of the true God, he cannot mean idols by his elohim, but the representations of divine things and symbols of the divine presence, the teraphim and ephod. Ellicott takes the opposite line. Micah does not scruple to call them his gods, as the idolater Laban had done, and the phrase looks meant to hold him up to scorn — the Greek softening it to my graven image and the Chaldee to my fear. To a Greek, who called a sculptor a god-maker, the phrase would have been unremarkable; on an Israelite's lips it is startling. Yet Ellicott ends generously, hoping Micah's loss proved his gain, and that he found the true God in the room of the gods he had made.

The answer he gets is a threat. Keil renders it an order to be silent on pain of life: let not thy voice be heard among us, lest men of savage disposition fall on thee and thou bring death on thyself and thy household. Ellicott gives the idiom literally, men bitter of soul, and notes that the phrase for losing life is properly gathering it. Clarke calls the argument what it is — a man must bear the loss of his substance or lose his life besides, the plain language of a highwayman. Gill has the Danites decline further talk with a man they thought impertinent, bidding him do his worst; and Keil closes the episode, Micah seeing they were stronger than he, and turning home.
27:
Henry opens with the moral of an unpunished march: meeting no disaster on the road, the Danites perhaps concluded they had done no wrong in robbing Micah — many justify themselves in their impiety by their prosperity. He then reads the state of Laish as a warning of the opposite kind: the people were quiet and secure, never suspicious of the five who had come to look them over, which made them easy prey to a handful of men; many are brought to destruction by their security, and Satan gets his advantage when we are careless, so that happy is the man who fears always. Clarke says the same more shortly, that the spies' report proved correct, the people apprehending no danger and unprepared to resist. Keil states it as the narrative does, that they fell upon a people living quietly and burned the city, which had no deliverer in its isolation. Henry notes that they met no resistance at all, and finds the reason in the ledger of two nations: the measure of Canaanite iniquity was full, while the Danites' was only beginning to fill.

Ellicott stops at the burning, which he calls unusual, Hazor being the one city Joshua is recorded to have burnt. He offers three possibilities — that they had devoted the place by a ban, as Jericho was devoted, or that the fire served some purpose of policy, or that it was accidental — and adds that the thought of such conduct being cruel probably never crossed their minds, so that we must not judge them by the standard of Christian times. He does not leave the tribe unjudged. Dan was no gainer by the conquest: the name drops out of the genealogies in Chronicles and is missing from the sealed tribes in the Revelation; and he cites Blunt's conjecture that the disappearance came of intermarriage with the Phoenicians.

On the isolation that doomed the town Gill and Clarke agree with the spies' own reasoning: Gill supposes Laish to have stood under Sidonian protection, so that the suddenness of the attack left no time to send for help, and Clarke that the Sidonians were simply too far off to be of use. Keil and Ellicott place the site between them. Keil sets it in the valley stretching to Beth-rehob, the upper part of the Huleh lowland through which the central source of the Jordan runs, and identifies Beth-rehob with the Rehob of the spies' report in Numbers. Ellicott puts it at the foot of the lowest range of Lebanon, notes that the name means house of spaciousness, and records Robinson's identification of it with Hunin, a fortress commanding the plain.

The renaming is read as a claim of kinship. Henry has them rebuild the city, the old buildings having gone to decay, and call it Dan as a witness that, separated as they now were by the length of the land, they were Danites by birth; and he draws the application, that we should be careful not to lose the privilege of our relation to God's Israel, but take every occasion to own it and preserve the memory of it for those who come after. Gill says the same, the name showing they belonged to a tribe far to the south-west. Clarke observes what the name afterwards became, one of the two ends of the land, the extent of the whole being commonly given as from Dan to Beersheba; Ellicott compares the Messenians, who changed Zankle into Messene. Henry closes on the irony of the settlement. God had kept his promise and put them in possession, which bound them to be faithful — they inherited the labour of the peoples that they might keep his statutes — and the first thing they did was to break them, attributing to an image a success which, had God been less patient, that image would have cost them.
30:
Gill supposes a house was built for the image in the new city, probably where Jeroboam afterwards set up one of his calves; the Danites, having prospered exactly as the oracle promised, held the things they had carried off in great veneration, and though only the graven image is named he takes it that the molten image, the teraphim and the ephod stood with it. Clarke says they erected a chapel of their own as Micah had, with the same furniture and the same priest. Ellicott presses the connection with Jeroboam: if this image was in the shape of a calf, the tradition of the cult may have made his innovation easier. He assumes the image was never dissociated from the worship of God, since Jonathan and the Danites name him Elohim, Micah for all his images calls him Jehovah, and the priest's own name means the gift of Jehovah.

The priest's grandfather is the chapter's textual crux, and both critics reach the same verdict. Clarke observes that no Manasseh will fit — not the son of Joseph, who had no son called Gershom, nor the king, who lived eight centuries later — and holds the word should be read Moses, as it stands in some manuscripts and in the Vulgate; the Jews suspended a letter above the word and the points did the rest, because they thought it a reproach to their legislator that his grandson should be an idolater. Ellicott sets out the mechanism: without the vowel points the two names differ by a single letter, and in the Masoretic text that letter is not boldly written but timidly and furtively suspended above the line, to hide the painful fact from the uninitiated. Rabbi Tanchum grants that Moses is written though Manasseh is read; and the Talmud, admitting the descent, says Scripture assigns him to Manasseh's family because he did Manasseh's deeds, a later rabbi explaining the suspended letter as making him son of Manasseh by imitation and son of Moses by blood. Ellicott will not have the sacred writer blamed for the pious fraud, which belongs to the Masoretic editors.

Whether Jonathan was the actual grandson Ellicott thinks scarcely doubtful, since he is contemporary with Phinehas, who was beyond question Aaron's own grandson. He finds in the speed of the fall — a young Levite hiring himself out for less than thirty shillings a year — a likely reason for the eclipse of the family of Moses, which never afterwards rose to any importance; Jonathan is left out of the Chronicler's list, unless he is the Shebuel whom Jerome takes him for, and Josephus omits the story altogether.

How long the thing lasted is fixed by the last verse. Clarke reports Calmet's conclusion that Jonathan's line served at Dan only while the house of the Lord stood at Shiloh, until the ark was taken by the Philistines in Eli's last year; and on that ground he passes on Houbigant's proposal that the text should read not the captivity of the land but the captivity of the ark, two letters being easily confounded. Ellicott corrects the English of the final verse, where the verb is not the one rendered set up just before but means that the image was entrusted to Jonathan's descendants; he dates the term by the sack of Shiloh, and suspects the verse was added by a later hand to prevent the earlier being misread. Clarke ends by refusing the charge of idolatry altogether. The Danites were the first dissenters from the established worship, but departed from its forms as little as they could, worshipping in the same manner though not the same place; better that, he thinks, than to be wholly destitute of the ordinances of God — and he believes they worshipped the true God according to their light, though the means they chose were not the best.
